situation: On holiday in Limbe, Rahila stands on the black sand beach. Big waves crash against the rocky coast. At the base of a rock face, the waves have cut a notch and small caves.
She hears the stones rolling in the water. Rahila wonders how water can be strong enough to break solid rock and carve these shapes.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is that Rahila does not understand how waves can break solid rock.
Why is the sand of Limbe black?
It comes from the volcanic rocks (basalt) of Mount Cameroon.
Why is it dangerous to sit under a sea cliff?
The waves undercut the cliff, and rocks can fall at any time.
end.justification: This lesson will help us to understand how waves erode rocky coasts and create cliffs, caves, arches and stacks.

qa.q: How does hydraulic action break a cliff?
qa.a: Waves hit the cliff and trap air in the cracks. The air is compressed, then expands suddenly when the wave goes back, and the rock breaks.

qa.q: What is the difference between abrasion and attrition on the coast?
qa.a: In abrasion, waves throw sand and stones against the cliff. In attrition, the stones hit each other and become small and round pebbles.

qa.q: What is solution (corrosion) on the coast?
qa.a: Sea water slowly dissolves some rocks, such as limestone and chalk.

sum.title: I. Erosional Processes of Waves
sum.intro: Waves erode the coast in four ways:
items: The Processes
– Hydraulic action: the force of waves and compressed air in cracks breaks the rock.
– Abrasion (corrasion): waves throw sand and stones against the cliff.
– Attrition: stones hit each other and become small, round pebbles.
– Solution (corrosion): sea water dissolves rocks such as limestone.

qa.title: Question 1
qa.q: How are capes and bays formed?
qa.a: Where hard and soft rocks meet the sea, waves erode the soft rock faster and form bays. The hard rock resists and sticks out as capes (headlands).

qa.title: Question 2
qa.q: Explain how a cliff and a wave-cut platform are formed.
qa.a: Waves cut a notch at the base of the rock. The rock above collapses and the cliff retreats. The flat rocky area left at its base is the wave-cut platform.

qa.q: Study the erosion of a headland.
Explain how a cave becomes an arch, then a stack and a stump.
qa.a: Waves enlarge a crack into a cave. The cave is cut through the headland and forms an arch. The top of the arch falls and leaves a stack. The stack is worn down into a stump.

sum.title: II. Erosional Features of Wave Action
sum.intro: Wave erosion forms the following features:
items: A. Capes and Bays
Soft rock is eroded faster and forms bays; hard rock resists and forms capes (headlands). Example: the bays and headlands around Limbe.
capes_bays.png
B. Cliffs and Wave-Cut Platforms
Waves cut a notch; the rock above collapses and the cliff retreats, leaving a flat wave-cut platform, seen at low tide.
cliff_platform.png
C. Caves, Arches, Stacks and Stumps
Waves enlarge a crack into a cave, then cut through to form an arch. The arch collapses and leaves a stack, which is worn into a stump.
headland_erosion.png

evaluation: It is the force of waves and compressed air in cracks, which breaks the rock.
Waves erode soft rock faster than hard rock, and form bays.
Put in order: stack, cave, stump, arch.
remediation: A piece of hard rock that sticks out into the sea is a ______.
A curved area of sea between capes is a ______.
The flat rock left at the foot of a cliff is a wave-cut ______.
A cave cut through a headland becomes an ______.
A pillar of rock separated from the land is a ______.
A small rock left after a stack collapses is a ______.
end.remediationAnswers: 1. cape (headland) 2. bay 3. platform 4. arch 5. stack 6. stump
end.homework: Put some sand at one end of a tray of water and make waves from one corner. Write where the sand moves.
